```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A transition network describes how the actors move between codes, but not
how often each code occurs in the first place. The two kinds of information
are read together. A transition out of a rare code can carry a high
probability on a handful of events, and a code that dominates one actor's
activity shapes the edges of the whole network. In a heterogeneous network
the frequencies have a further role: they show how each actor divides its
activity over its own codes, which is the first description of the division
of labor between a human and an AI.

This guide covers two summaries that precede and accompany the network. The
frequency tables and plots give the distribution of the codes within each
actor and over the whole interaction. The mosaic plot gives the joint
distribution of consecutive codes, with each cell shaded by how far its count
departs from the count expected if the next code did not depend on the
current one.

```{r package}
library(htna)
```

## Data

`human_ai` holds 429 sessions of human-AI pair programming; each row is one
coded event.

- **Session**: `session_id`.
- **Code**: `code`; six human and six AI codes.
- **Actor type**: `actor_type`, `"Human"` or `"AI"`.
- **Order**: `order_in_session`.

The frequency summaries use the relative network. The mosaic tests counts,
so it needs the network of transition counts (`method = "frequency"`).

```{r build}
data(human_ai)
net <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")
net_counts <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type",
                         method = "frequency")
```

## How does each actor divide its activity?

`frequencies_htna()` counts every code and reports it under its actor, with
its share of that actor's events. The shares sum to one within each actor.

```{r frequencies}
frequencies_htna(net)
```

The AI's activity is concentrated: executions are 38.1% of its events and
asks 28.3%, while delegations (3.45%) and repairs (3.01%) are rare. The
human's activity is spread over requests (28.8%), specifications (27.1%) and
expressions of frustration (16.9%). Edges out of `Delegate` and `Repair`
rest on fewer than 300 events each and have wider intervals than edges out
of `Execute` (see [Model assessment](model-assessment.html)).

The treemap shows the same table, one panel per actor, with each tile's area
proportional to the code's share of its actor.

```{r treemap}
plot_frequencies_htna(net)
```

## Which codes dominate the interaction as a whole?

`state_frequencies_htna()` gives the pooled table: each code's share of all
events, whichever actor produced it.

```{r pooled}
state_frequencies_htna(net)
```

Pooled over both actors, the AI's executions (16.8% of all events) and the
human's requests (16.0%) and specifications (15.1%) together make up almost
half of the interaction. The bar view puts both actors on one axis, sorted by
count and coloured by actor, for this comparison across actors.

```{r bars}
plot_frequencies_htna(net, view = "bars")
```

Because the two actors produce different numbers of events, the faceted
view, with a separate axis per actor, is the better display when
the question is the profile within each actor.

```{r facet}
plot_frequencies_htna(net, view = "facet")
```

## Which transitions occur more often than chance?

`mosaic_plot_htna()` draws the table of consecutive codes, source codes in
columns and target codes stacked within them. The width of a column is the
share of transitions from that code and the height of a tile the share of
its target, so the area of a tile is the share of that transition. Each tile
is shaded by its standardised residual against independence of source and
target: blue tiles are transitions that occur more often than independence
predicts, red tiles less often. The residuals are estimated by permutation (500 permutations by default),
which needs no large-sample approximation; `residuals = "asymptotic"` gives the closed-form chi-square
residuals instead. The axis labels are coloured by actor. Clipping the colour
scale to plus or minus 4 keeps a few extreme cells from washing out the rest.

```{r mosaic, fig.height = 6}
mosaic_plot_htna(net_counts, range = c(-4, 4), seed = 1L)
```

The mosaic is the cell-level counterpart of the turn-taking templates of the
[Sequences and patterns](sequences-and-patterns.html) guide, where handovers
between the actors occur 1.22 to 1.28 times as often as independence
predicts; here each tile shows which specific pair of codes carries that
excess. Reading the network together with the mosaic distinguishes a strong
edge that is strong because its target is common from one that is strong
because the source specifically leads to it.

## Which summary to use

| Question | Function |
|---|---|
| How does each actor divide its activity over its codes? | `frequencies_htna()`, `plot_frequencies_htna()` |
| Which codes dominate the whole interaction? | `state_frequencies_htna()`, `plot_frequencies_htna(view = "bars")` |
| Within-actor profiles when the actors differ in volume | `plot_frequencies_htna(view = "facet")` |
| Which consecutive pairs occur more or less often than chance? | `mosaic_plot_htna()` on a frequency network |
